Advanced · lesson 2

One archetype table

src/2.archetype_table/archetype_table.rin

src/2.archetype_table/archetype_table.rin

Eight sparks in one table with three component columns, positions, velocities and lives, plus a numbers column that exists only so the output can say which spark is which. Each frame they move, they age, and the ones that ran out are removed.

Two rules

Columns never disagree. spark_spawn and spark_despawn are the only places rows come and go, and each touches every column. A new component means a new column, one line in each of those two procs, and one more argument to spark_spawn. A call site cannot add a row to some columns and forget the others.

Rows are packed. Systems loop over 0..count and never test whether a row is alive. Removing a row moves the last row into the hole:

spark 0 in row 0 expired; spark 7 moved from row 7 into it

That one copy per column is the whole cost of a despawn, whatever the table's size. The price is that a row number is not a name for a spark. After that line, "row 0" means spark 7. Lesson 4 adds names that do not move.

Removing while iterating

expire_system walks the rows backwards. When it removes row i, the row that moves in comes from the end, and the end has already been tested. A forward loop would have to stay on i after a removal, and it is easy to get wrong. Lesson 6 removes the question entirely by not removing anything during a loop.

Systems take slices

move_system(positions: noalias []vec2, velocities: []const vec2, dt) gets the rows in use, sparks.positions[0..sparks.count], and knows nothing about tables. []const says it only reads velocities. Each positions[i] is bounds checked in Debug, against the count rather than the capacity, so a system that runs past the live rows stops with a message instead of reading stale data.

noalias says that for the call, nothing else reaches the memory positions covers. Only the column the system writes needs it: a promise on the written column already rules out a write landing in the column being read. Without it, clang -O2 and gcc -O3 both vectorized this loop behind a run-time check that the two columns are apart. With it, neither checks. A Debug build checks the promise instead, once per call.

age_system(lives: noalias []f32, dt) has one slice, and still takes it. Windows passes a slice by reference, as a pointer to a copy, and clang-cl does not use C's type rules to decide what can overlap. So without the promise, a float written through lives might be the slice's own pointer or length. clang-cl then reads both again after every element and does one float at a time. With it, the loop is eight floats per pass:

movups (%rcx,%r8,4), %xmm2         four lives
movups 0x10(%rcx,%r8,4), %xmm3     four more
subps  %xmm0, %xmm2                minus dt
subps  %xmm0, %xmm3
movups %xmm2, (%rcx,%r8,4)
movups %xmm3, 0x10(%rcx,%r8,4)

The rule that holds on every compiler: noalias on every slice a loop writes, even when it is the only one.

lives is the one column here that is a plain run of floats. positions and velocities are vec2, x and y side by side, so move_system's vector loop spends some of its instructions pulling the x's and the y's apart. Lesson 1 measures what that costs.

Status codes

spark_spawn returns spawn_status, an enum[must_use]: calling it and ignoring the result is a compile error. That is rin's convention for a proc that can fail: a status, with the result through an out-parameter. The ninth spark shows the full case.

Try

  1. Rewrite expire_system to walk forwards with a plain for. The output does not change, because no frame here expires a spark together with the one in the last row. Change two lives so that one does, and find the spark that outlives its life by a frame. Then fix the loop.
  2. Delete the line in spark_despawn that copies lives. What does the output show, and how long did it take to notice?
  3. Call spark_spawn without using its result and read the compiler's error. Then discard it on purpose with _ = spark_spawn(...).
  4. Make the table grow instead of reporting full: allocate double the capacity from the arena and copy every column across. Lesson 4's kayan_table_grow is one answer.

Advanced · lesson 3

Many archetypes

src/3.many_archetypes/many_archetypes.rin

src/3.many_archetypes/many_archetypes.rin

Four archetypes (rock, ship, bullet, turret) and four components (position, velocity, health, damage). One table type holds all four archetypes, and two queries decide which tables each system visits.

A table without a type

Lesson 2's table had one typed field per column. That cannot work for every archetype at once, so the columns become bytes:

table: struct = {
    signature: u64;
    count: u64;
    capacity: u64;
    columns: [component<>.count][*]u8;
}

columns[id] is null when the table has no such component. Its element size is component_info[id][0].size, where component_info holds each component's reflect record, position<>& and so on. table_add_row and lesson 4's moves work only from sizes, so they never need to know a component's type.

Types come back at the edges. column<T>(t) asks component_of<T>() for T's id, casts that column to [*]T, and returns it as a []T of the rows in use. component_of is one specialisation per component, one line each. Systems take []position, []velocity and so on, exactly as in lesson 2.

Sized by reflection

component has no count member at the end. component<>.count is the number of members, from the enum's reflect record, and it sizes both columns and component_info. With a hand-added count member the reflected count is one more than the number of components. That is how the bounds check found a bug while this lesson was being written.

components_check compares each enum member's name with the name in component_info. Swap two entries in component_info and the program stops before anything runs:

component 2 is health in the enum but damage in component_info

Different types, fewer checks

move_system takes noalias []position, as lesson 2's takes noalias []vec2, and for the same reason. regen_system takes noalias []health, its only slice, for the reason lesson 2 gives for age_system.

One difference showed before either had noalias: clang on Linux vectorized this move_system without a run-time overlap check, and lesson 2's only with one. Here the two columns are different struct types, position and velocity, and clang reads C's type rules as saying they cannot share memory; built with -fno-strict-aliasing, it checks here too. In lesson 2 both are vec2. gcc checked in both. clang-cl, rin's default compiler, does not use those rules at all, to match MSVC, so on Windows both lessons were checked. noalias makes the answer the same everywhere, whatever the column types are.

Queries

moving: query = { .all = bit(component.position) | bit(component.velocity) };
healing: query = { .all = bit(component.health), .none = bit(component.damage) };

A table matches when it has every bit in all and none in none. moving visits ships and bullets. healing visits ships but not turrets, which have health but also deal damage. The output prints each visit.

The signature cannot lie

table_create builds the signature from the component list it allocates columns for. kayan wrote them separately, and archetype D's signature left out two of its columns (see 0_from_kayan.md).

Try

  1. Add an armor component, give it to turrets, and make a query that visits only tables with both health and armor.
  2. Ask a rock for column<velocity>. Read the message, then find where it comes from.
  3. Change columns to [4][*]u8. Then add a fifth component and see what happens, and where.
  4. Write table_remove_row with the swap-remove from lesson 2, working only from component_info sizes and memcpy.

Advanced · lesson 4

Entity handles

src/4.entity_handles/entity_handles.rin

src/4.entity_handles/entity_handles.rin, includes/kayan.rin

The world: tables made on demand, entity handles that survive row moves, despawning with index reuse, and moving an entity between archetypes when a component is added or removed. The code is includes/kayan.rin. The lesson program calls each part and prints what happened.

Handles, slots, rows

kayan_entity: struct = { index: u32; generation: u32; }
kayan_slot:   struct = { generation: u32; table: u32; row: u32; }

A handle is what the rest of a program keeps. Its index picks a slot, and the slot says where the entity lives now. Rows move all the time: every despawn and every archetype change swap-removes. When one does, the table's entities column says which entity owned the moved row, and that entity's slot gets the new row number. Handles never change.

generation is what makes a handle safe to keep after its entity dies. Despawning bumps the slot's generation and frees the index, and the next spawn reuses the index with the new generation:

spawn d: it reuses a's index with the next generation
    d = 0:2 in table 0 row 2 {position velocity} at (4.0, 0.0)
    a = 0:1 is dead

kayan_alive is one comparison: the handle's generation against the slot's. A free slot already holds its next generation, which no handle carries yet, so no separate "alive" flag is needed. a cannot reach d's data, kayan_get returns null for it, and despawning it again returns kayan_status.dead and changes nothing.

Generations start at 1. A zeroed handle, {}, is 0:0, which never matches a slot, so it can stand for "no entity" without a separate flag.

Statuses

kayan_despawn, kayan_add, kayan_remove and kayan_move return kayan_status, an enum[must_use]: ok, or dead when the handle no longer names a live entity. Ignoring one is a compile error. The lesson discards them on purpose with _ = kayan_add<health>(...) where the handle is known to be alive.

Tables on demand

kayan_table_for(w, signature) looks the signature up in a hashmap<u64, u32> and makes the table if it is new. Nobody declares archetypes; they appear when an entity first needs that combination. Tables live in a vec<kayan_table> and are referred to by index, because adding one can move the whole list.

Tables start with room for 16 rows and double when full. The old columns stay in the arena unused, which is a waste these lessons accept. The last part of the program spawns 40 entities so the first table grows twice, despawns every other one, and checks the result two ways.

Checking the world

Reading back each survivor's position is a weak check. Swap-remove copies rows, so a stale row often still holds the right numbers. kayan_verify checks the invariant instead: every row of every table belongs to a live entity whose slot points back at that table and row, and the rows add up to the live count. It prints each problem it finds and returns how many there were. The lesson prints kayan_verify: 0 problems and fails if that is not so.

kayan_get also checks the slot's row against the rows in use, so in Debug a slot that points past the end of its table stops the program at the first lookup.

Moving between archetypes

give b health: b moves to a new table and keeps its position

kayan_add<health> computes signature | bit(health), finds or makes that table, appends a row, copies every component the two tables share, then swap-removes the old row. kayan_remove is the same move with the bit cleared. A move costs two row copies, one into the new table and one to fill the hole in the old, so components that come and go every frame are better as a field than as a component. A burning flag in health, say, instead of a burning component.

Try

  1. Despawn b and keep using its handle. Which calls notice, and which would not if kayan_alive did not check the generation?
  2. Remove the line in kayan_table_remove_row that updates the moved entity's slot. In Debug the program stops at the first kayan_get through a stale row. Build it with -DNDEBUG and run it again: the position check still says all 20 are fine, and kayan_verify lists every broken slot.
  3. At the end of the lesson, table 0 has 22 rows and room for 64. Hold a []position from kayan_column, spawn at least 43 more so the table grows, then write through the old slice and read the position back through kayan_get. The write is lost, and nothing reports it. That stale slice is why lesson 6 defers spawns.
  4. Add kayan_has<T>(w, e) -> b32 without moving anything.

Imports the world from includes/kayan.rin.

1// 4. Entity handles2//3// Lesson 2 ended on a problem: swap-remove keeps a table packed, but it moves4// rows, so "spark 7 is row 7" stops being true the moment something before it5// dies. Anything that remembers an entity by its row (a target, a parent, a UI6// selection) ends up pointing at whoever moved in.7//8// The fix is one level of indirection that does not move:9//10//   * A handle is {index, generation}. The index picks a slot in the world's11//     slot list; the slot says which table and row the entity is in now.12//   * Every table keeps an `entities` column: the handle that owns each row.13//     When a swap-remove moves the last row, that column says whose slot to14//     update. That is the line lesson 2 could not write.15//   * Despawning bumps the slot's generation and puts the index on a free list.16//     The next spawn reuses the index with the new generation, so every old17//     handle to the dead entity fails the generation check instead of quietly18//     finding the newcomer. Advanced · lesson 5

The inspector

src/5.inspector/inspector.rin

src/5.inspector/inspector.rin

A soldier and a crate, printed field by field by code that names no component type, then edited by component and field name, then a table layout report. Everything comes from the reflect records the world already holds for sizes.

What a reflect record has

T<> is a reflect record: name, size, align, kind, count, and for a struct, count fields. Each field has its name, offset, size, type ("f32" for a builtin, "array_16_c8" for a [16]c8), elem_type and array_count for arrays, and info, the record of the field's own type when it has one. A nested struct or an enum field has info; a builtin like f32 does not.

print_fields walks that. It takes the component's bytes as a []const u8, from kayan_get_bytes, and cuts each field's bytes out of it by offset and size, so a record that disagreed with the data would stop the program in Debug. Struct fields recurse through info, enum fields print their member name through reflect_name_from_value_or, a [16]c8 prints as text, and builtins print by type name. Because components are structs, even a single float like health.points has a name to print.

Tags

health: struct = { points: f32; max: f32; regen_timer: f32 @ "hidden"; }

@ "hidden" is a string attached to the field, read with reflect_field_has_attr. The inspector skips it. The component decides what a tool shows, and the tool does not need to know the component.

Names belong in tools

set_f32_by_name(w, e, "health", "points", 55.0) finds the component by name, the field by name, checks the field is an f32, and writes it. It refuses weapon.ammo, a u32, and the crate's health, which it does not have. That is the flexibility an editor or a console needs. It is also the string comparison kayan did in every query, once per archetype. Here it runs once per edit, and systems keep using ids.

Layout

print_layout lists each table's columns with size and alignment, and each column's bytes in use out of the bytes allocated for the table's capacity. It is the kind of report that shows when a component has grown padding, when a table has far more room than rows, or when a table carries a column most of its systems never read.

Try

  1. Add a bool-like b32 field to weapon and teach print_builtin to print it as yes or no.
  2. Give position a @ "readonly" tag and make set_f32_by_name refuse fields that carry it.
  3. Write set_by_name for u32 and i32 as well, picking the write from field.type.
  4. Print a whole table as rows and columns: one line per entity, one column per field.

Advanced · lesson 6

kayan

src/6.kayan/kayan.rin

src/6.kayan/kayan.rin

A turret at the centre, five wings of three drones, 140 frames. Seven systems run each frame, and every structural change they want goes through a command buffer applied at the end of the frame.

The frame

spawner    wings of drones enter                    records spawns
turret     shoot at the nearest drone               records spawns
movement   position += velocity * dt                writes
lifetime   bullets expire                           records despawns
collision  live bullets against drones              writes health, records despawn and add
burning    burning drones lose health               writes
outcome    destroy dead drones, catch leaks         records despawns
  blast    a destroyed drone hurts its neighbours   writes health, records adds
apply      every recorded change, in order

Writes to components happen in place, during queries. Changes to which table an entity is in are recorded, and applied once nothing is iterating.

Lifetime runs before collision, and collision skips bullets whose lifetime is used up. Those bullets are only still in their table because nothing structural happens until the end of the frame. Without the skip, a bullet that hit on its last frame would be despawned twice and counted as both a hit and a miss.

Systems and kernels

movement_system and burning_system are each a query and a kernel:

integrate: proc(ps: noalias []position, vs: []const velocity, dt: f32) -> void
burn: proc(hs: noalias []health, bs: []const burning, dt: f32) -> void

The system walks the tables and calls the kernel once for each table that matches. The kernel sees two columns, so the compiler sees a straight loop over two arrays. noalias qualifies parameters, so the loop needs a proc of its own to carry it; that is the only reason these two are split out. The output does not change.

Before the split, gcc -O3 vectorized both loops behind a run-time check that the columns were apart. After it, without the check. clang on Linux had no check either way, for the reason lesson 3 gives: the columns are different types. clang-cl, which does not use C's type rules, needs noalias here too.

burn is the cleanest loop in the game. health and burning are each one f32, so their columns are plain runs of floats, and the kernel is eight floats per pass with nothing to rearrange: loads, mulps, subps, stores. integrate works on vec2s and spends some of each pass separating x from y; lesson 1 shows what the fully split layout looks like.

integrate and burn are streams: every row of every matching table, in order. collision_system and blast_system are closer to lookups: for each bullet or each blast, they visit drones that could be anywhere. Lesson 7 measures what each layout costs for both kinds of loop, and why the components here stay small structs.

lifetime_system stays one proc. Its loop records a despawn for each expired bullet, and a loop that calls something per row is not vectorized whatever its parameters say. The other systems branch, search or record in their loops too.

Why not change tables during a query

Each of these would be a real bug with the world from lesson 4:

  • Despawn. The swap-remove moves the last row into the hole, behind the loop, so that entity is not processed this frame. Meanwhile the slice the system cut before the despawn still reaches the old last row, a stale copy, and anything written to it is lost.
  • Spawn. A table that is full grows, and its columns move to new memory. A system holding a []position from before the spawn keeps writing to the old copy. Nothing crashes; the writes are just lost.
  • Add or remove. The entity moves to another table, which the same query may reach later. That entity is processed twice this frame.

The buffer

command: struct = { kind; entity; pending; signature; id; payload; }

Spawned entities have no handle until the buffer runs, so commands_spawn returns a pending number, and commands_set_spawned<T> writes a component into "the entity that pending spawn will create". T has to be in the spawn's signature, and applying the buffer stops the program with a message if it is not. Payloads are copies of the component value, kept as a []u8 in the buffer's frame arena next to the commands. commands_apply runs everything in order, then clears the arena. One memops_arena_clear frees the whole frame's commands.

Skipped commands

Frame 113 is the interesting one. A bullet destroys one drone, and its blast takes two burning neighbours below zero in the same loop. Each of them is destroyed in turn, and each blast reaches back to drones already recorded as destroyed:

bullet 8:9 hits drone 6:1, health -13.2
drone 6:1 is destroyed
drone 7:1 is caught in the blast, health -14.4
drone 4:2 is caught in the blast, health -4.8
drone 7:1 is destroyed
drone 6:1 is caught in the blast, health -54.0
...

The blast cannot know 6:1 is doomed: its despawn is only recorded, and it is still in its table. So it records an add<burning> against it. When the buffer is applied the despawn comes first, and kayan_move reports kayan_status.dead for the add, so the command is skipped. The summary counts three.

Try

  1. Call kayan_despawn directly in outcome_system instead of recording it. The first difference is at frame 56: the program reports drone 3:1 destroyed, but the drone it removed was 1:1. Explain why, from the swap-remove and the slices the loop is holding.
  2. Make blast_system skip neighbours whose health is already at or below zero. The skip count drops to zero. Is the buffer's check still needed?
  3. Give the turret a health component and let leaking drones damage it. When it reaches zero, despawn it through the buffer and end the game.
  4. Print the buffer before applying it, as a log of every structural change the frame made.
  5. Inline integrate back into movement_system, build with gcc -O3 -fopt-info-vec, and find the loop it now versions for aliasing.
  6. Run with --sanitize after each change. A stale slice into a grown table is exactly what AddressSanitizer does not catch, because the old memory is still valid arena memory. Think about what would.

Imports the world from includes/kayan.rin.

Bullets hurt drones, a badly hurt drone5// catches fire, and a drone at zero health is destroyed in a blast that hurts6// and ignites the drones around it. A drone that reaches the turret is a leak.7//8// The new idea is when structural changes happen. Spawning, despawning, adding9// and removing components all change tables, and systems are in the middle of10// walking tables when they decide to make those changes:11//12//   * a despawn swap-removes: the last row moves into the hole, behind the13//     loop, so that entity is not processed this frame, while a slice cut14//     before the despawn still reaches the old last row, a stale copy whose15//     writes are lost;16//   * a spawn can grow a table, which moves every column of it to new memory,17//     while the system still holds a slice of the old one;18//   * an add or a remove moves an entity into another table, which the same19//     query may walk later, so the entity is visited twice.20//21// So systems do not make structural changes. They record them in a command22// buffer, and the frame applies the buffer once every system has run. Plain23// writes to components are fine during a query: a hit lowers a drone's health24// in place. Only changes to which table an entity is in wait for the end of25// the frame.26//27// The buffer lives in a frame arena. Commands and their payloads are pushed28// into it during the frame and the whole arena is cleared after it is applied,29// so nothing in it is freed one at a time. Advanced · lesson 7

Layout follows access

src/7.access_patterns/access_patterns.rin

src/7.access_patterns/access_patterns.rin

Lesson 1 found the layout SIMD wants: one array per float. This lesson asks what that layout costs everywhere else. 1,048,576 bodies are stored four ways, and two kinds of loop run over each, and the program checks that all four end with the same positions.

Two kinds of loop

Stream: every body, in order, the same math. Integration is the example:

for (i: u64 = 0; i < px.length; i += 1) {
    px[i] += vx[i] * dt;
    ...
}

The next body is always right after the last one, so the hardware prefetcher has it ready, and SIMD can take four or eight at once if they sit side by side.

Lookup: bodies picked by index, two at a time, in no particular order. Contacts are the example, the way collision and constraints reach bodies:

a: u64 = cast(cs[c].a, u64);
b: u64 = cast(cs[c].b, u64);
dx: f32 = px[b] - px[a];
...

Each body is somewhere else in memory. What matters is how many cache lines one body's data sits in, because each one is a separate trip to memory. SIMD does not help: there are no four neighbours to load at once.

Four layouts

aos      [ x y z vx vy vz m r ][ x y z vx vy vz m r ] ...      32 bytes a body
columns  positions  [ x y z ][ x y z ][ x y z ] ...
         velocities [ vx vy vz ][ vx vy vz ] ...                 24 bytes a body
split    px [ x x x x ... ]   py [ y y y y ... ]   pz ...  vx ...  vy ...  vz ...
blocks   [ x0..x7 | y0..y7 | z0..z7 | vx0..vx7 | vy0..vy7 | vz0..vz7 ][ x8..x15 ...
  • aos keeps everything about a body together, two fields neither loop uses included.
  • columns is one array per component, each component a small struct. This is what an ECS table stores, and what lessons 2 to 6 use.
  • split is one array per float, lesson 1's move_split.
  • blocks is eight bodies at a time, each coordinate a run of eight floats. It is split cut into pieces of eight, with the pieces of one body kept near each other. The usual name is AoSoA, an array of structs of arrays.

The program prints how many 64-byte cache lines one body's position sits in:

cache lines one lookup touches: aos 1.000, columns 1.125, split 3.000, blocks 2.000

A 12-byte vec3 crosses a line boundary 2 times in 16, hence 1.125. In split, x, y and z are in three different arrays. In a block, x and y share a line and z is in the next.

Measured

Release, clang -O2, best of three runs, on the 2.8 GHz Xeon these lessons were checked on: 4 MB of L2, 33 MB of L3. The body count was changed in the generated C for the first and last columns. At 65,536 bodies each layout fits in L2; at the lesson's 1,048,576 each is about the size of L3; at 8,388,608 each is 192 to 256 MB and comes from RAM.

Stream, ns per body:

layout65,5361,048,5768,388,608
aos1.674.204.09
columns1.682.082.88
split0.931.301.66
blocks0.701.622.79

Lookup, ns per contact:

layout65,5361,048,5768,388,608
aos5.0326.2750.35
columns3.4211.9440.35
split6.5428.2295.01
blocks5.9825.7061.20

clang with -mavx2 -mfma and gcc -O3 agree on the main points: split streams fastest from RAM, columns look up fastest at every size, and split looks up slowest from RAM. Where two numbers are within about 20 percent, the order changes from build to build; gcc -O3, for one, streamed columns fastest at a million bodies. The machine is shared; expect about 20 percent noise.

What it says:

  • Split wins the stream and loses the lookup. From RAM it streams 1.7 times faster than columns, and looks up 2.4 times slower: three lines a body instead of one.
  • Columns win the lookup everywhere and come second or third in the stream. AoS also has one line a body, but its bodies are 32 bytes, so the same lookups spread over more memory. At a million bodies, columns' positions are 12 MB and sit comfortably in L3; AoS spreads them over 32 MB, about all of it.
  • Blocks are the compromise. In L2 they streamed fastest of all, and a little behind split at a million bodies. They look up better than split at every size. From RAM their stream fell back to about columns' speed on this machine, which I have not explained.
  • Out of cache, a lookup costs ten to fifty times a streamed body. From RAM, 40 to 95 ns a contact against 2 to 4 ns a body. Turning lookups into something closer to a stream, by sorting contacts or walking space in order, usually saves more than any layout choice.

What the compiler makes of it

clang-cl /O2, Windows x64, from the object file:

loopbodies a passinstructions a passshuffles
integrate_aos1161
integrate_columns47730
integrate_split4200
integrate_blocks8370
integrate_split, /arch:AVX28140
integrate_blocks, /arch:AVX28140
contacts_columns1 contact250
contacts_split1 contact320

Blocks vectorize as cleanly as split: the inner loop over eight lanes is a fixed-size loop over consecutive floats, which compilers turn into whole registers. The contact loops are one contact a pass in every layout.

In between

Engines that have both kinds of loop do one of these:

  • Blocks, as above. One layout, decent at both.
  • Gather, work, scatter. Storage stays in columns or AoS, good for lookups. The hot loop copies a batch of bodies into a wide layout, x's in one register and y's in another, does its math, and copies them back. The copy pays off when the same batch is worked on many times, as a constraint solver does over several iterations. Box2D v3 solves contacts this way, four or eight at a time.
  • Two layouts for two jobs. A particle system that only ever streams stores split. The bodies that collision looks up stay in columns.

How an ECS decides

An ECS does not decide where each float goes. The component is the unit it stores together, and the programmer decides what a component is.

  • Tables. kayan, Unity's entities, Bevy and flecs keep one table per archetype, with one column per component. That is this lesson's columns layout: an array per component, and each component's fields side by side inside it. Unity cuts its tables into 16 KB chunks, each holding every component array for as many entities as fit, which is close to blocks at the level of components.
  • Sparse sets. EnTT stores each component in its own dense array with a lookup table from entity to index, and can keep several components in the same order ("groups") so a system over them streams. Bevy lets each component choose: table storage, or a sparse set for components added and removed often.
  • Systems are streams. A system is a query and a kernel, as in lesson 6: the ECS finds the tables that match, and hands the kernel each table's columns. That stream over columns is the fast path every ECS is built for. Systems that say which columns they read and which they write are what lets a scheduler run them in parallel.
  • Lookups go through the handle. Reaching one entity is handle, slot, table and row, then the column: kayan_get in lesson 4. That is this lesson's lookup loop with an extra hop in front. ECS code keeps lookups for the places that need them, such as relationships between entities and collision, and finds the rest by query.

So the decisions that are yours:

  1. Keep components small, to what one stream system reads. A component a system reads half of is AoS's wasted bytes again.
  2. Leave components as small structs, position { x, y, z }, unless a profiler shows a stream over them is the bottleneck. They are the best layout for lookups and good enough for most streams.
  3. For a hot stream over huge counts, particles above all, store split or blocks, or gather into them for the hot loop.
  4. Make lookups rarer and less random before tuning their layout.

Try

  1. Sort cs by a before the timing loops and run --time again. Which lookup numbers change, and by how much?
  2. Set body_count and contact_count to 8388608 and run --time in Release. Compare with the tables above.
  3. Make the contacts push velocities too, vx, vy and vz of both bodies. How many lines does a lookup touch in each layout now?
  4. Add /arch:AVX2 to build_c_flags and compare the stream column.
  5. Write contacts_gather: for every eight contacts, copy the sixteen bodies' positions into [8]f32 arrays, do the arithmetic over the arrays, and copy back. Contacts that share a body in the same eight break it; find the case and decide what to do about it.
  6. Make body 64 bytes with fields neither loop uses, and watch aos in both tables.

s < steps; s += 1) { contacts_blocks(blocks, cs); }349    t[8] = seconds();350 351    printfmt("{} bodies, {} contacts, {} steps\n", body_count, contact_count, steps);352    printfmt("bytes per body: aos {}, columns {}, split {}, blocks {}\n",353        sizeof(body), sizeof(vec3) * 2, sizeof(f32) * 6, sizeof(body_block) / 8);354    printf("cache lines one lookup touches: aos %.3f, columns %.3f, split %.3f, blocks %.3f\n",355        lines_per_lookup(0), lines_per_lookup(1), lines_per_lookup(2), lines_per_lookup(3));356 357    sums: [4]f64 = {358        checksum_aos(aos),359        checksum_columns(col.positions),360        checksum_split(spl.px, spl.py, spl.pz),361        checksum_blocks(blocks),362    };363    printf("checksum aos %.3f\n", sums[0]);364    printf("checksum columns %.3f\n", sums[1]);365    printf("checksum split %.3f\n", sums[2]);366    printf("checksum blocks %.3f\n", sums[3]);367    same: b32 = sums[0] == sums[1] && sums[1] == sums[2] && sums[2] == sums[3];368    printfmt("same result: {}\n", same ? "yes" : "no");369 370    if (timing) {371        n_stream: f64 = cast(body_count * steps, f64);372        n_lookup: f64 = cast(contact_count * steps, f64);373        printf("ns per body     stream   ns per contact   lookup\n");374        printf("  aos           %6.2f                    %6.2f\n", (t[1] - t[0]) * 1.0e9 / n_stream, (t[2] - t[1]) * 1.0e9 / n_lookup);375        printf("  columns       %6.2f                    %6.2f\n", (t[3] - t[2]) * 1.0e9 / n_stream, (t[4] - t[3]) * 1.0e9 / n_lookup);376        printf("  split         %6.2f                    %6.2f\n", (t[5] - t[4]) * 1.0e9 / n_stream, (t[6] - t[5]) * 1.0e9 / n_lookup);377        printf("  blocks        %6.2f                    %6.2f\n", (t[7] - t[6]) * 1.0e9 / n_stream, (t[8] - t[7]) * 1.0e9 / n_lookup);378    }379    return same ? 0 : 1;380}

1// kayan: archetype tables, entity handles, and moving entities between tables.2//3// This is the world lesson 4 builds, kept as a library so lessons 5 and 6 can4// use it as it is. Read it with lesson 4: the lesson explains the why, this5// file is the how.6//7// What a program using it provides:8//9//   * its components, as structs, and an enum with one member per component;10//   * `component_of: proc<T>() -> <its enum>` for each component type, which11//     the generic procs here call to find a type's id;12//   * a call to `kayan_register` for each component, with its reflect record.13//14// Ids are u32 here, so the library does not need to know the program's enum.15// Up to 64 components, because a signature is a u64.16//17// Not here, on purpose: threads, change tracking, chunked storage, relations.18// Each is worth a lesson of its own and none is needed to see the idea.19 20import "std/print.rin"21import "std/memops.rin"22import "std/vec.rin"23import "std/hashmap.rin"24 25// A handle. `index` picks a slot in the world's slot list and `generation` says26// which life of that slot the handle was made for. Despawning bumps the slot's27// generation, so every handle to the dead entity stops matching, even after the28// index is reused. Generations start at 1, so a zeroed handle, `{}`, never29// names a live entity and can stand for "none".30kayan_entity: struct = {31    index: u32;32    generation: u32;33}34 35// Where an entity lives now: which table, which row. Rows move (swap-remove,36// lesson 2), so this is updated whenever one does. Handles never move. A free37// slot already holds its next generation, which no handle has yet, so the38// generation check alone says whether a handle is alive.39kayan_slot: struct = {40    generation: u32;41    table: u32;42    row: u32;43}44 45// One archetype. `entities[row]` is the handle of the entity in that row, which46// is how a swap-remove finds the slot to fix. `columns[id]` is null unless the47// signature has bit `id`.48kayan_table: struct = {49    signature: u64;50    count: u64;51    capacity: u64;52    entities: [*]kayan_entity;53    columns: [64][*]u8;54}55 56kayan_query: struct = {57    all: u64;58    none: u64;59}60 61// What a structural change reports. `dead` means the handle no longer names a62// live entity, so nothing was changed.63kayan_status: enum[must_use] = {64    ok,65    dead,66}67 68kayan_world: struct = {69    arena: *memops_arena;70    infos: [64]*const reflect;71    component_count: u32;72    // Tables are referred to by index. A pointer from kayan_table_at is good73    // until the next table is created, which can move the list.74    tables: vec<kayan_table>;75    by_signature: hashmap<u64, u32>;76    slots: vec<kayan_slot>;77    free: vec<u32>;78    live: u64;79}80 81// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------82// Components83// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------84 85kayan_bit: proc(id: u32) -> u64 = {86    return 1'u64 shl cast(id, u64);87}88 89kayan_id_of: proc<T>() -> u32 = {90    return cast(component_of<T>(), u32);91}92 93kayan_mask_of: proc<T>() -> u64 = {94    return kayan_bit(kayan_id_of<T>());95}96 97kayan_world_init: proc(w: *kayan_world, arena: *memops_arena) -> void = {98    w[0] = {};99    w[0].arena = arena;100}101 102kayan_register: proc(w: *kayan_world, id: u32, info: *const reflect) -> void = {103    if (id >= 64) {104        printfmt("kayan: component id {} is past the 64 a signature can hold\n", id);105        exit(1);106    }107    w[0].infos[id] = info;108    if (id + 1 > w[0].component_count) {109        w[0].component_count = id + 1;110    }111}112 113kayan_component_name: proc(w: *kayan_world, id: u32) -> [*]const char = {114    return w[0].infos[id][0].name;115}116 117// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------118// Tables119// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------120 121kayan_table_at: proc(w: *kayan_world, index: u32) -> *kayan_table = {122    return vec<kayan_table>at(w[0].tables&, cast(index, u64));123}124 125// Double the table's columns. The old columns stay in the arena unused: an126// arena does not free single allocations, and these lessons accept the waste.127kayan_table_grow: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table) -> void = {128    capacity: u64 = t[0].capacity == 0 ? 16 : t[0].capacity * 2;129    entities: [*]kayan_entity = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(w[0].arena,130        sizeof(kayan_entity) * capacity, alignof(kayan_entity)), [*]kayan_entity);131    if (t[0].count > 0) {132        memcpy(entities[0]&, t[0].entities[0]&, sizeof(kayan_entity) * t[0].count);133    }134    t[0].entities = entities;135    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w[0].component_count; id += 1) {136        if ((t[0].signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {137            info: *const reflect = w[0].infos[id];138            column: [*]u8 = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(w[0].arena, info[0].size * capacity,139                info[0].align), [*]u8);140            if (t[0].count > 0) {141                memcpy(column[0]&, t[0].columns[id][0]&, info[0].size * t[0].count);142            }143            t[0].columns[id] = column;144        }145    }146    t[0].capacity = capacity;147}148 149// The table for a signature, made the first time anything needs it.150kayan_table_for: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> u32 = {151    found: *u32 = hashmap<u64, u32>get(w[0].by_signature&, signature);152    if (found != null) {153        return found[0];154    }155    for (id: u32 = 0; id < 64; id += 1) {156        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0 && (id >= w[0].component_count || w[0].infos[id] == null)) {157            printfmt("kayan: signature {} uses component {}, which was never registered\n", signature, id);158            exit(1);159        }160    }161    t: kayan_table = {};162    t.signature = signature;163    index: u32 = cast(w[0].tables.length, u32);164    vec<kayan_table>append(w[0].arena, w[0].tables&, t);165    hashmap<u64, u32>put(w[0].arena, w[0].by_signature&, signature, index);166    return index;167}168 169// A new row with zeroed components, owned by `e`.170kayan_table_add_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {171    if (t[0].count == t[0].capacity) {172        kayan_table_grow(w, t);173    }174    row: u64 = t[0].count;175    t[0].entities[row] = e;176    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w[0].component_count; id += 1) {177        if (t[0].columns[id] != null) {178            size: u64 = w[0].infos[id][0].size;179            memset(t[0].columns[id][row * size]&, 0, size);180        }181    }182    t[0].count += 1;183    return row;184}185 186// Swap-remove: the last row moves into `row`, and the slot of the entity that187// moved is told its new row. This is the line lesson 2 could not write.188kayan_table_remove_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table, row: u64) -> void = {189    last: u64 = t[0].count - 1;190    if (row != last) {191        for (id: u32 = 0; id < w[0].component_count; id += 1) {192            if (t[0].columns[id] != null) {193                size: u64 = w[0].infos[id][0].size;194                memcpy(t[0].columns[id][row * size]&, t[0].columns[id][last * size]&, size);195            }196        }197        moved: kayan_entity = t[0].entities[last];198        t[0].entities[row] = moved;199        vec<kayan_slot>at(w[0].slots&, cast(moved.index, u64))[0].row = cast(row, u32);200    }201    t[0].count = last;202}203 204kayan_matches: proc(t: *kayan_table, q: kayan_query) -> b32 = {205    return (t[0].signature & q.all) == q.all && (t[0].signature & q.none) == 0;206}207 208// T's column, cut to the rows in use. Asking for a column the table does not209// have is a bug in the caller, so it stops the program.210kayan_column: proc<T>(t: *kayan_table) -> []T = {211    id: u32 = kayan_id_of<T>();212    if (t[0].columns[id] == null) {213        printfmt("kayan: table {} has no column for component {}\n", t[0].signature, id);214        exit(1);215    }216    raw: [*]T = cast(t[0].columns[id], [*]T);217    return raw[0..t[0].count];218}219 220kayan_table_entities: proc(t: *kayan_table) -> []kayan_entity = {221    return t[0].entities[0..t[0].count];222}223 224// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------225// Entities226// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------227 228kayan_alive: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {229    if (cast(e.index, u64) >= w[0].slots.length) {230        return 0;231    }232    return vec<kayan_slot>at(w[0].slots&, cast(e.index, u64))[0].generation == e.generation;233}234 235// A new entity with the components in `signature`, all zeroed. A freed index is236// reused before a new one is made, with the generation its despawn left behind.237kayan_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> kayan_entity = {238    e: kayan_entity = {};239    if (!vec<u32>is_empty(w[0].free&)) {240        e.index = vec<u32>pop(w[0].free&);241    } else {242        e.index = cast(w[0].slots.length, u32);243        vec<kayan_slot>append(w[0].arena, w[0].slots&, { .generation = 1 });244    }245    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w[0].slots&, cast(e.index, u64));246    e.generation = slot[0].generation;247 248    table_index: u32 = kayan_table_for(w, signature);249    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, table_index);250    row: u64 = kayan_table_add_row(w, t, e);251 252    slot[0].table = table_index;253    slot[0].row = cast(row, u32);254    w[0].live += 1;255    return e;256}257 258// A dead handle reports `dead`, so despawning twice is harmless.259kayan_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {260    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {261        return kayan_status.dead;262    }263    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w[0].slots&, cast(e.index, u64));264    kayan_table_remove_row(w, kayan_table_at(w, slot[0].table), cast(slot[0].row, u64));265    slot[0].generation += 1;266    vec<u32>append(w[0].arena, w[0].free&, e.index);267    w[0].live -= 1;268    return kayan_status.ok;269}270 271kayan_signature: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {272    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {273        return 0;274    }275    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w[0].slots&, cast(e.index, u64));276    return kayan_table_at(w, slot[0].table)[0].signature;277}278 279// Move `e` to the table for `signature`. Build and check

tools/check.py runs every program and diffs its output

block.group(1))]56 57 58def run(cmd: list[str], cwd: Path = ROOT) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess[str]:59    return subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=cwd, text=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE,60                          stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, timeout=300)61 62 63def check(rin: Path, cc: str, lesson: Path, bless: bool, sanitize: bool) -> tuple[bool, str]:64    stem = lesson.stem65    work = OUT / stem66    work.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)67    c_path = work / f"{stem}.c"68    exe = work / (f"{stem}.exe" if os.name == "nt" else stem)69 70    translate = run([str(rin), "compile", str(lesson), "-o", str(c_path),71                     "--header", str(work / f"{stem}.h")])72    noise = [line for line in translate.stdout.splitlines()73             if line.strip() and not line.startswith("rin: generated")]74    if translate.returncode != 0 or noise:75        return False, "rin compile:\n" + translate.stdout76 77    flags = ["-std=c11", "-g", "-Wall", "-Wextra", "-Werror"]78    if sanitize:79        flags += ["-fsanitize=address,undefined", "-fno-sanitize-recover=all"]80    includes = ["-I", str(rin.parent), "-I", str(rin.parent / "std")]81    libs = [] if os.name == "nt" else ["-lm"]82    build = run([cc, *flags, *includes, str(c_path), "-o", str(exe), *libs])83    if build.returncode != 0 or build.stdout.strip():84        return False, f"{cc}:\n" + build.stdout85 86    ran = run([str(exe)])87    if ran.returncode != 0:88        return False, f"exit {ran.returncode}:\n{ran.stdout}"89 90    actual = ran.stdout.replace("\r\n", "\n")91    expected_path = lesson.with_suffix(".expected")92    if bless:93        expected_path.write_text(actual, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")94        return True, "blessed"95    if not expected_path.exists():96        return False, f"no {expected_path.name}; run with --bless after reading the output:\n{actual}"97    expected = expected_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").replace("\r\n", "\n")98    if actual !=
